notes: Sample restore_config.json - the backup jobs the toolkit runs, and the restores that prove them. Copy to restore_config.json and edit.

Two lists, and the second is the point. 'backups' takes backups; 'restores' restores them somewhere else and checks the result. A backup nobody has restored is a hope, not a recovery plan, which is why they live in one file and are configured together.

Nothing here names a host or a credential twice: every entry points at db_instances.json by 'server_id' (or by 'id' on a restore's source and target), and the address, container, transport and account are resolved from there. Change a machine in one place.

'env_secrets' maps an environment variable the backup script needs to a key in data/encrypted_secret_text.json. The value is decrypted into the child process's environment and never written to a file or an argument list - an argument is world-readable in the process table.

'jobs' is one entry per backup kind, each with its own schedule and retention, so a full and a log backup of the same database are independent. 'time_window' and 'notify' are the same shared objects used everywhere else.

A restore entry's 'databases' list scopes what is restored. An empty list means 'everything found', which quietly goes on restoring ageing files after a database is removed from the source plan - name them explicitly unless you want that.

'target_retention_seconds' is how long a restored copy is kept before it is dropped. A drill target is disposable by design; keeping copies indefinitely fills the target instance and turns a proof into an incident.

A physical restore carries the SOURCE instance's logins and passwords with it. After a drill the target answers to the source's credentials, and the target's own stored credential goes stale - expect that rather than being surprised by it.

backup_restore._note: Which files are worth copying off a backup share, and how far back to look. A wider window means recopying files that are already there; a narrower one means missing a backup taken late.

backups.note: Full backup of the application instance. The SSH or WinRM transport, the credential and the address all come from db_instances.json via server_id.

jobs._note: A separate job because the log backup is what sets the recovery point objective. Every fifteen minutes, all day - if this schedule and backup_policy.json disagree, the report is right and one of them is wrong.

backups.note: Weekly baseline plus daily incrementals; the script picks the level from the day of the week. 'backup_dir' must match the directory the archive metric checks, or a cluster that is backed up daily is reported as never backed up.

restores.note: The drill. It restores yesterday's backup onto a disposable instance, verifies it, and drops the copy a day later. Scoped to the databases that matter - an empty list would go on restoring whatever it found, including files nobody produces any more.

server_metadata.note: Replays the source instance's server-level metadata - logins, roles, Agent jobs - around the database restore, so the restored databases have no orphaned users. It reads a bundle written by that instance's own backup entry, so turning it on without one only produces a warning every run.
